```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_metafor)
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
}
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# Bounds in the text are rounded outward, so that they stay true.
up <- function(x, digits = 2) num(ceiling(x * 10^digits - 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
down <- function(x, digits = 2) num(floor(x * 10^digits + 1e-9) / 10^digits, digits)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
```

In a random-effects meta-analysis the studies play the part of the sites.
A study's reliability is the weight that its own estimate keeps in the
empirical Bayes prediction of its true effect, and poolinfo's diagnostics
summarize these weights over the studies. In this vignette we fit a
meta-analysis with metafor [@viechtbauer2010] and compute the diagnostics
in three ways: at metafor's estimate of the between-study variance, over a
confidence interval for it, and over its posterior. Along the way we
relate them to the heterogeneity statistics that metafor prints. For the
definitions of $I$, $\bar S$, $H$, $V$ and $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (the
informativeness, the mean reliability, the dispersion, the logit variance
and the concentration count), see `vignette("poolinfo")`.

`r if (!has_metafor) "The rest of this vignette needs the metafor package, which is not installed."`

```{r library, message = FALSE}
library(poolinfo)
library(metafor)
```

```{r without-metafor, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
if (!has_metafor) knitr::knit_exit()
```

metafor writes the between-study variance $\tau^2$, and poolinfo writes it
$\sigma_\tau^2$ (`sigma_tau^2` in its printed output). We use poolinfo's
notation from here on, so $\sigma_\tau$ is the between-study standard
deviation. poolinfo's printed output calls the studies sites.

## A meta-analysis of teacher expectancy effects

We use the data set `dat.raudenbush1985` of the metadat package, which
metafor loads. It has `r nrow(dat.raudenbush1985)` studies of the effect
of teachers' expectations on their pupils' IQ, each with a standardized
mean difference and its sampling variance
[@raudenbush1984; @raudenbush1985]. We fit the usual random-effects model
by restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

```{r fit}
dat <- dat.raudenbush1985
fit <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML")
fit
```

```{r fit-facts, include = FALSE}
s2 <- typical_variance(se2 = dat$vi)
gm <- exp(mean(log(dat$vi)))
I2_Q <- (fit$QE - (fit$k - 1)) / fit$QE
fit_dl <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "DL")
stopifnot(
  abs(fit$I2 / 100 - fit$tau2 / (fit$tau2 + s2)) < 1e-10,
  abs(fit_dl$I2 / 100 - I2_Q) < 1e-10,
  abs(I2_Q - fit$I2 / 100) > 0.05,
  abs(fit$H2 - 1 / (1 - fit$I2 / 100)) < 1e-10,
  s2 < gm
)
# The typical variance can be below or above the geometric mean.
gm_of <- function(v) exp(mean(log(v)))
stopifnot(typical_variance(se2 = c(1, 1, 100)) < gm_of(c(1, 1, 100)),
          typical_variance(se2 = c(1, 100, 100)) > gm_of(c(1, 100, 100)))
```

metafor estimates $\sigma_\tau^2$ at `r num(fit$tau2, 4)` and reports
$I^2 = `r num(fit$I2, 1)`\%$ and $H^2 = `r num(fit$H2)`$. As a proportion,
its $I^2$ is $\hat\sigma_\tau^2 / (\hat\sigma_\tau^2 + v_{\mathrm{typ}})$,
where $v_{\mathrm{typ}}$, `r num(s2, 4)` here, is the "typical"
within-study variance of
@higgins2002, which `typical_variance()` also computes. The familiar
$(Q - \mathrm{df})/Q$, here `r num(I2_Q)`, agrees with it only when
$\sigma_\tau^2$ is estimated by the DerSimonian-Laird method
[@dersimonian1986], as the note
in `?metafor::print.rma` explains. metafor's $H^2$ is $1/(1 - I^2)$, the
ratio of the total variability to the sampling variability, and it has
nothing to do with poolinfo's dispersion $H$.

## The profile at the REML estimate

`reliability_profile()` takes the fit, computes the studies' reliabilities
at metafor's estimate of $\sigma_\tau$, and summarizes them.

```{r profile}
profile <- reliability_profile(fit)
profile
```

```{r profile-facts, include = FALSE}
mu <- c(coef(fit))
stopifnot(
  max(abs(blup(fit)$pred - (mu + profile$S * (dat$yi - mu)))) < 1e-10,
  profile$stats[["I"]] < fit$I2 / 100,
  fit$se.tau2 > 0.75 * fit$tau2
)
```

At the REML estimate, $I$ is `r num(profile$stats[["I"]])`, below
metafor's $I^2$ of `r num(fit$I2 / 100)`, although both divide
$\sigma_\tau^2$ by $\sigma_\tau^2$ plus a representative sampling
variance. $I$ uses the geometric mean of the sampling variances,
`r num(gm, 4)`, which here is larger than the typical variance (with other
variances it can be smaller). So $I$ is the reliability of a study whose
sampling variance is that geometric mean, and also what we get by
averaging the studies' reliabilities on the logit scale and transforming
back [@lee2026]. Across the studies, the reliabilities range from
`r num(min(profile$S))` to `r num(max(profile$S))`. Each is the weight
that a study's own estimate keeps in its empirical Bayes prediction:
`blup(fit)` returns $\hat\mu + S_j (y_j - \hat\mu)$ for study $j$, with
$\hat\mu$ the estimated mean effect.

A profile at one value of $\sigma_\tau$ carries no uncertainty about that
value, and with `r fit$k` studies the uncertainty is large. metafor's
standard error of $\hat\sigma_\tau^2$, `r num(fit$se.tau2, 4)`, is
`r pct(fit$se.tau2 / fit$tau2)`% of the estimate itself.

## Confidence intervals mapped through the diagnostics

$I$ and $\bar S$ increase with $\sigma_\tau^2$, and so does $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$
when the sampling variances differ, as they do here. A confidence interval
for $\sigma_\tau^2$ therefore maps to an interval for each of them with the
same coverage. $H$ first rises and then falls, so its interval is the range
of $H$ over the interval for $\sigma_\tau^2$, which covers the true value at
least as often. `map_tau2_interval()` maps the Q-profile interval of
@viechtbauer2007, which `confint()` also reports for this fit up to its
default tolerance, and keeps it as an attribute.

```{r mapped}
mapped <- map_tau2_interval(fit)
mapped
attr(mapped, "interval")
```

metafor's `confint()` maps the same Q-profile interval through its own
$I^2$:

```{r confint}
confint(fit)
```

```{r mapped-facts, include = FALSE}
at_I <- function(m, col) m[[col]][m$functional == "I"]
qp <- attr(mapped, "interval")
ci <- confint(fit, control = list(tol = 1e-12, maxiter = 1000))$random
stopifnot(
  abs(qp[["lower"]] - ci["tau^2", "ci.lb"]) < 1e-8,
  abs(qp[["upper"]] - ci["tau^2", "ci.ub"]) < 1e-6,
  qp[["lower"]] > 0,
  at_I(mapped, "lower") < profile$stats[["I"]],
  at_I(mapped, "upper") > 0.8
)
```

The Q-profile interval for $\sigma_\tau^2$ runs from
`r num(qp[["lower"]], 4)` to `r num(qp[["upper"]], 4)`. Through $I$ it
becomes a 95% confidence interval from `r num(at_I(mapped, "lower"))` to
`r num(at_I(mapped, "upper"))`, and through metafor's $I^2$ an interval
from `r pct(ci["I^2(%)", "ci.lb"] / 100)`% to
`r pct(ci["I^2(%)", "ci.ub"] / 100)`%. Both intervals have the coverage of
the Q-profile interval and differ only in the representative sampling
variance. Like everything else in poolinfo, they are conditional on the
sampling variances.

## The posterior and the restricted likelihood

`reliability_posterior()` takes the fit too. It computes the posterior of
the diagnostics with flat priors on the mean and on $\sigma_\tau$, the
package's default, which `vignette("posterior-summaries")` discusses.

```{r posterior}
post <- reliability_posterior(fit)
post
```

```{r posterior-facts, include = FALSE}
pp <- profile_summary(post)
val <- function(q, col = "mean") pp[[col]][pp$quantity == q]
# Under the flat priors, the posterior density of sigma_tau is proportional
# to the restricted likelihood, whose peak is at the REML estimate.
ll <- function(tau2) {
  c(logLik(rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML", tau2 = tau2)))
}
ratio_0 <- exp(ll(0) - ll(fit$tau2))
dens <- functional_density(post, "sigma_tau", n = 4000)
peak <- dens$value[which.max(dens$density)]
at <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
from_density <- approx(dens$value, dens$density, xout = at)$y /
  max(dens$density)
from_likelihood <- exp(sapply(at^2, ll) - ll(fit$tau2))
stopifnot(
  val("I", "lower") < 0.01, prob_above(post) < 0.5,
  abs(peak - sqrt(fit$tau2)) < 0.002,
  max(abs(from_density - from_likelihood)) < 0.005,
  ratio_0 > 0.5, fit$QEp < 0.025
)
```

With a posterior mean of `r num(val("I"))` and a 95% posterior interval
from `r num(val("I", "lower"), 3)` to `r num(val("I", "upper"))`, the
posterior of $I$ reaches values near 0, although the Q-profile interval for
$\sigma_\tau^2$ excludes 0. Each interval rests on a different statistic. With a flat prior on the mean,
integrating the mean out of the likelihood leaves the restricted
likelihood that REML maximizes [@harville1974]. Since the prior on $\sigma_\tau$ is flat
too, the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ is proportional to that
restricted likelihood. Its peak is at the REML estimate,
$\hat\sigma_\tau = `r num(sqrt(fit$tau2), 3)`$, and at $\sigma_\tau = 0$
the density is still `r num(ratio_0)` of the peak. Cochran's $Q$, on which
the Q-profile interval is built, is `r num(fit$QE, 1)` at
$\sigma_\tau^2 = 0$, on `r fit$k - 1` degrees of freedom
($p = `r num(fit$QEp, 3)`$).

A confidence interval built on the restricted likelihood behaves like the
posterior. metafor's profile likelihood interval, which
`?metafor::confint.rma` describes as more consistent with REML estimation,
includes 0, and we map it through the diagnostics by giving
`map_tau2_interval()` the sampling variances and the interval.

```{r profile-likelihood}
pl <- confint(fit, type = "PL")$random["tau^2", ]
mapped_pl <- map_tau2_interval(se2 = dat$vi, interval = c(
  estimate = fit$tau2, lower = pl[["ci.lb"]], upper = pl[["ci.ub"]]
))
mapped_pl
```

```{r profile-likelihood-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(pl[["ci.lb"]] == 0, at_I(mapped_pl, "lower") == 0,
          abs(at_I(mapped_pl, "upper") - val("I", "upper")) < 0.05,
          at_I(mapped_pl, "upper") < at_I(mapped, "upper"))
```

Mapped through $I$, the profile likelihood interval runs from
`r num(at_I(mapped_pl, "lower"))` to `r num(at_I(mapped_pl, "upper"))`,
close to the posterior interval from `r num(val("I", "lower"), 3)` to
`r num(val("I", "upper"))`, whereas the Q-profile interval gave
`r num(at_I(mapped, "lower"))` to `r num(at_I(mapped, "upper"))`.

## A proper prior

With `r fit$k` studies we also want to know how much the flat prior on
$\sigma_\tau$ contributes. A half-normal prior with scale 0.5 is a
reasonable proper alternative for standardized mean differences. It puts
95% of its mass below `r num(0.5 * qnorm(0.975))`, so it allows true
effects that vary from study to study by up to about one standard
deviation of IQ and makes larger spreads unlikely. `prior_sensitivity()`
refits the posterior under it and sets the two fits side by side.

```{r prior}
prior_sensitivity(post, list(
  `half-normal, scale 0.5` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.5)
))
```

```{r prior-facts, include = FALSE}
half_normal <- update(post, prior = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.5))
ph <- profile_summary(half_normal)
hn <- function(q, col = "mean") ph[[col]][ph$quantity == q]
stopifnot(abs(hn("I") - val("I")) < 0.02,
          abs(hn("I", "upper") - val("I", "upper")) < 0.02)
```

With this prior, $I$ has a posterior mean of `r num(hn("I"), 3)` rather
than `r num(val("I"), 3)`, and its 95% posterior interval ends at
`r num(hn("I", "upper"), 3)` rather than `r num(val("I", "upper"), 3)`.
For these studies, then, our reading of the posterior is the same under
either prior.

## A moderator

With moderators, $\sigma_\tau^2$ is the residual heterogeneity, the
variance of the true effects around the meta-regression, and each study is
pulled toward its own predicted value. @raudenbush1984 related the effects
to the weeks of contact between teachers and pupils before the
expectations were induced. As in the example on the help page of
`dat.raudenbush1985`, we cap the weeks at 3, so that the moderator
distinguishes 0, 1, 2, and 3 or more weeks.

```{r moderator}
dat$weeks.c <- pmin(dat$weeks, 3)
fit_weeks <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ weeks.c, data = dat, method = "REML")
fit_weeks
```

```{r moderator-facts, include = FALSE}
S_weeks <- reliability_profile(fit_weeks)$S
stopifnot(fit_weeks$tau2 < 1e-4, fit_weeks$R2 > 99, fit_weeks$QEp > 0.4,
          max(S_weeks) < 1e-3)
```

The REML estimate of the residual $\sigma_\tau^2$ falls from
`r num(fit$tau2, 4)` to `r num(fit_weeks$tau2, 4)`, metafor's $R^2$ is
`r round(fit_weeks$R2)`%, and the test for residual heterogeneity gives
$p = `r num(fit_weeks$QEp)`$. At that estimate the largest study
reliability is `r formatC(max(S_weeks), format = "f", digits = 5)`, so
the profile at the REML estimate would pull every study all the way to its
predicted value. Under the flat priors, the posterior instead weights each
value of $\sigma_\tau$ by its restricted likelihood, as we saw above, and
we fit it for the meta-regression next.

```{r moderator-posterior}
post_weeks <- reliability_posterior(fit_weeks)
post_weeks
```

```{r moderator-posterior-facts, include = FALSE}
pw <- profile_summary(post_weeks)
wk <- function(q, col = "mean") pw[[col]][pw$quantity == q]
stopifnot(wk("I") < val("I") / 2, wk("I", "upper") < 0.5,
          wk("sigma_tau") < val("sigma_tau") / 2,
          all(post_weeks$checks$status == "ok"))
```

With the moderator, the posterior mean of $I$ falls from
`r num(val("I"))` to `r num(wk("I"))`, with a 95% posterior interval from
`r num(wk("I", "lower"))` to `r num(wk("I", "upper"))`, and the posterior
mean of $\sigma_\tau$ from `r num(val("sigma_tau"), 3)` to
`r num(wk("sigma_tau"), 3)`. Once the moderator accounts for most of the
variation of the true effects, little of what remains can be told apart
from sampling error. The model then pulls each study most of the way
toward its predicted value. Now the flat prior is on the two coefficients
of the meta-regression, and the printed output lists their posterior means
and intervals.

## The studies' reliabilities

Here the sampling variances range from `r num(min(dat$vi), 4)` to
`r num(max(dat$vi), 4)`, a `r round(max(dat$vi) / min(dat$vi))`-fold
range, and their logit variance is $V = `r num(val("V"))`$. We plot the
reliabilities of the model without the moderator, sorted, with their 95%
posterior intervals.

```{r plot-profile, fig.alt = sprintf("The posterior means of the %d study reliabilities, sorted from %s to %s, with their 95%% posterior intervals, the informativeness and its 95%% posterior band, and the mean reliability.", fit$k, num(min(site_table(post)$reliability)), num(max(site_table(post)$reliability)))}
plot_profile(post)
```

```{r plot-profile-facts, include = FALSE}
sites <- site_table(post)
low <- sites$site[sites$reliability == min(sites$reliability)]
high <- sites$site[sites$reliability == max(sites$reliability)]
stopifnot(identical(low, "4"), identical(high, "18"),
          which.max(dat$vi) == 4L, which.min(dat$vi) == 18L,
          all(sites$reliability_lower < 0.02),
          all(sites$reliability_upper - sites$reliability_lower > 0.45))
```

Study `r low`, by `r dat$author[as.integer(low)]`, has the largest
sampling variance and a posterior mean reliability of
`r num(min(sites$reliability))`, and study `r high`, by
`r dat$author[as.integer(high)]`, has the smallest variance and
`r num(max(sites$reliability))`. Every study's posterior interval starts
below `r up(max(sites$reliability_lower))` and is at least
`r down(min(sites$reliability_upper - sites$reliability_lower))` long,
because the posterior of $\sigma_\tau$ is wide, and the band of $I$ runs
from `r num(val("I", "lower"), 3)` to `r num(val("I", "upper"))`.

## Your own meta-analysis

With your own meta-analysis, you pass the `rma()` fit to

- `reliability_profile()` for the profile at its estimate,
- `map_tau2_interval()` for confidence intervals, or
- `reliability_posterior()` for the posterior, where its moderators
  become the mean model.

poolinfo reads fits of `rma.uni()`, the function behind `rma()`, which
have one between-study variance and independent estimates. If your studies
give several estimates each, you would model them with `rma.mv()`, whose
fits poolinfo does not read. One option is then to combine the estimates
of each study into one with metafor's `aggregate()` method for `escalc()`
data, under an assumed correlation within studies, and to fit `rma()` to
the result.
